rewrites.summary:
Wyoming's March 2025 facility bans signed into law cover sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities plus school restrooms, so a trans traveler using any public restroom or changing room faces legal exposure.

The July 2026 per-state legal-risk assessment lists Wyoming among 'the worst states' for legislation targeting transgender adults.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National policy changes keep creating legal difficulties for transgender people across the states, per the July 2026 assessment's national frame.
rewrites.localsOnly: Senate File 62 applies to public school children from pre-kindergarten up and charter-school students, requiring restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth; districts must provide a 'reasonable accommodation' to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender recorded at birth.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The national tracker page behind the facility-ban enumeration is unreachable (404); the facility-ban years rest on the research dossier's extract.

rewrites.summary:
West Virginia's March 2025 facility restriction has an unusually wide reach - K-12 schools, higher education, corrections and domestic-violence shelters - so a trans visitor can meet it well beyond restrooms.

The July 2026 legal-risk assessment places West Virginia in the worst-law group, and the dossier scores it below the national score 0.36.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The assessment's 'Worst Policies In Effect' national frame and worst-state grouping colour any visit; the same update recorded other states moving into starker tiers.
rewrites.localsOnly: Senate Bill 456, signed March 12, 2025, defines 'woman' as an adult human of the female sex and 'man' as an adult human of the male sex and aims to preserve single-sex spaces including locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories and prisons.

rewrites.summary:
Arkansas confines trans students to birth-sex school facilities under a March 2023 law (HB 1156) that remains in force and was extended in 2025; its school focus means a visitor's direct exposure is narrower than in states with adult-reaching bans.

The July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading lists Arkansas among the worst states.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation over the state's ban on gender-affirming care for minors continues: an en-banc review of an injunction reversal is pending.
rewrites.localsOnly: The ban on gender-affirming care for minors, first enacted in 2021 and still challenged, governs resident healthcare; state law has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The national tracker page behind the facility-ban enumeration is unreachable, so the enumeration rests on the dossier; the care-ban litigation outcome is unresolved (en-banc review of the injunction reversal pending).

rewrites.summary:
Ohio enacted a law in 2024 governing public bathroom and facility use by sex assigned at birth; signed November 27, 2024 and effective February 25, 2025, it requires K-12 schools and colleges to make students use bathrooms and locker rooms matching the sex on their birth certificates and carries no enforcement mechanism, so visitors meet it mostly on campuses.

An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment lists Ohio among its worst group of states for transgender adults.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The same assessment frames its findings as 'Worst Policies In Effect' nationally.
rewrites.localsOnly: The 'Protect All Students Act' (Senate Bill 104) requires public and private schools, colleges and universities to designate separate bathrooms, locker rooms and overnight accommodations by sex; the governor signed it out of public view over the objections of teachers' unions and civil rights groups, and it took effect in 90 days.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The national tracker page cited for the ban's category has moved from its cited URL, so the tracker-based classification cannot be re-verified from that link.

rewrites.summary:
Iowa's 2023 public-facility-use law applies to everyone on school grounds - including visitors - requiring restrooms and changing areas to match the sex on the birth certificate, with single-person facilities available to students who obtain written guardian consent.

The July 2026 legal-risk assessment lists Iowa among its worst states for transgender adults; a September 2026 status check confirmed the facility law and the minor-care ban remain in force.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Independent analysts of the same period caution that legal-risk grades predict how the state behaves toward trans people, not how residents do, and that recorded violence counts are undercount floors.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Senate File 538 bars doctors from administering gender-affirming care to anyone under 18 and remains in force; the second statute, Senate File 482, restricts which school restrooms and changing rooms students may use.

State courts kept Medicaid surgery coverage available to transgender adults, striking down the parallel ban on adult surgery coverage - a partial carve-back - through a March 2019 ruling.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The national tracker page behind the facility-ban enumeration is unreachable (404); violence figures cited as interpretive context are undercount estimates rather than verified totals.

rewrites.summary:
South Carolina's facility ban, enacted 2024, was expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities when the governor signed House Bill 4756 on May 15, 2026, requiring students in public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching sex assigned at birth.

The July 2026 assessment counts the expansion, raising the state's tier to 'Worst Laws Passed'; South Carolina is part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group and scores below the national score 0.36.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The July 2026 assessment's national frame is 'Worst Policies In Effect', and its rubric ranks states by reading the adult and youth law text.
rewrites.localsOnly: House Bill 4756 governs students across K-12 and higher education; the Senate amended the bill before passage, and the state's civil-liberties chapter framed it as discrimination against trans students.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The dossier's 'Worst Laws Passed' tier label sits uneasily beside the assessment's own wording that the state is 'among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier'.

The 18-state grouping defining sex by birth is asserted in the current text, but no surviving source in this record's list supports it.

rewrites.summary:
A gubernatorial executive order (August 30, 2023) narrows the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female', declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, ends state recognition of transgender people, and backs single-sex spaces for bathrooms and changing rooms - mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity.

Below the national score 0.36.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Legal observers recorded that opponents questioned the order's scope and legality when it was signed.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The executive order's direct bite is on state legal recognition - birth records, marker documentation and how state systems read a trans person's legal sex - which is resident-facing; what a visitor feels is the signal that state machinery is aimed at gender identity.

The order establishes the Women's Bill of Rights and directs state agencies to apply 'biological' definitions of sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The national news report behind the claim that state recognition has ended was unreachable (403) at fetch time, so that characterization rests on the dossier note; the 0.36 benchmark has no surviving source in this record's list.

rewrites.summary: Kentucky enacted a school-focused facility restriction in 2023 (K-12) that governs which restrooms students may use in public schools; for a visitor, direct exposure is limited by the law's school setting, but the statute places Kentucky in the group of states that have legislated against transgender facility use.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Federal litigation over the same 2023 statute produced a dated outcome: a federal judge lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, letting the ban on gender-affirming care for minors take effect on July 14, 2023.

Senate Bill 150, enacted March 29, 2023 after the legislature overrode the governor's veto, bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors and restricts which bathrooms those students can use in public schools.

The state's education department issued April 2023 guidance for districts implementing the rules, including caution on the bathroom-ban provisions.
